title: Module 7 Misconception Sort
intro: Decide whether each statement is true, false, or depends. These are the misconceptions that cost students points on exams.

items.s: The t distribution is the same as the normal distribution.
items.why: It resembles the normal curve but has heavier tails, especially for small df.

items.s: With the same data, a one-sample t test gives a larger critical value than the corresponding z test.
items.why: Estimating sigma from s adds uncertainty, so the cutoff moves farther out.

items.s: A larger sample always gives a larger t.
items.why: A larger n shrinks the standard error, which tends to raise t, but t also depends on the size of the difference and on s.

items.s: Cohen's d depends on the sample size.
items.why: d uses s as the standardizer, not the standard error, so it does not shrink or grow with n.

items.s: If the 95 percent CI for the mean difference contains zero, the effect is exactly zero.
items.why: The CI contains zero as one plausible value. The true difference could still be nonzero.

items.s: The one-sample t test requires that the population is normal, or that n is reasonably large.
items.why: Normality of the sampling distribution of the mean is the key assumption.

items.s: We can find the exact p value for t from the t table.
items.why: The t table shows critical values for selected alpha levels. Software gives exact p values.

items.s: The degrees of freedom for a one-sample t test equal the sample size.
